presentingComplaint: Progressively worsening breathlessness over 4 days, now unable to lie flat, with 2-pillow orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea last night.
history: 68-year-old man with known ischaemic HFrEF (prior anterior STEMI 3 years ago, echo 18 months ago showed LVEF 30%) on losartan, bisoprolol, spironolactone and furosemide, presents with 4 days of progressive exertional dyspnoea now present at rest, orthopnoea requiring 2 pillows, and one episode of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea last night that woke him gasping for air. He reports 3 kg weight gain over the past week and bilateral ankle swelling. He admits to dietary indiscretion (salty food at a family function) and says he ran out of furosemide 5 days ago. No chest pain, no fevers, no cough with purulent sputum, no recent illness. No palpitations. No dysuria or diarrhoea.
examination: Sitting bolt upright, visibly breathless at rest, using accessory muscles. Cool peripheries, mild diaphoresis. Raised JVP to angle of jaw. Bilateral fine basal crackles extending to mid-zones. Displaced apex beat, S3 gallop present. Bilateral pitting pedal oedema to mid-shin. No calf tenderness. Abdomen soft, mild hepatomegaly, no ascites. No rash, no fever.

labs.troponin_note: mildly elevated, non-rising on serial testing — demand-type, no dynamic ischaemic change
labs.venousBloodGas: mild respiratory alkalosis, no significant hypercapnia

imaging: CXR: cardiomegaly, bilateral perihilar haziness, upper lobe venous diversion, Kerley B lines, small bilateral pleural effusions — consistent with pulmonary venous congestion
ECG: sinus tachycardia, poor R-wave progression and Q waves in anterior leads consistent with old anterior MI, no acute ST-T changes
Bedside echocardiogram: severely reduced LVEF ~25-30%, global hypokinesia with anteroapical akinesia (old infarct), moderate functional mitral regurgitation, dilated IVC with reduced collapsibility
differentialDiagnoses: Acute decompensated heart failure (HFrEF) due to dietary/medication non-adherence
Acute coronary syndrome with new heart failure
finalDiagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), pulmonary congestion, precipitated by dietary sodium indiscretion and diuretic non-adherence
citations: Harrison 22e — Heart Failure: Pathophysiology and Diagnosis
ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure 2021
AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure 2022
contraindications: Avoid NSAIDs (worsen fluid retention and renal function)
Avoid non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (negative inotropic effect) in HFrEF
Use IV nitrates cautiously if hypotensive; avoid if SBP <90-100 mmHg
Avoid excessive/rapid diuresis if evidence of concomitant hypoperfusion (cardiorenal syndrome risk)
Do not abruptly stop beta-blocker unless cardiogenic shock present
edgeCases: Mildly elevated non-rising troponin is common in acute decompensated HF from demand ischaemia/wall stress and does not by itself indicate acute coronary syndrome — serial troponins and ECG needed to exclude ACS as precipitant
Worsening renal function with diuresis (cardiorenal syndrome) may require balancing decongestion against renal perfusion rather than stopping diuretics outright
If SpO2 fails to improve with initial therapy or work of breathing worsens, escalate to non-invasive ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP)
Hyponatraemia (133 mmol/L) reflects neurohormonal activation (dilutional) in chronic HF and usually improves with decongestion rather than fluid restriction alone
This condition (heart_failure) maps to a broader ICD category than the specific HFrEF/pulmonary-congestion phenotype described; acceptableIds reflect the general heart_failure entity
expectedMaiK: MaiK should recognise classic acute decompensated HFrEF with pulmonary congestion (orthopnoea, PND, raised JVP, bilateral crackles, S3, cardiomegaly with venous congestion on CXR, markedly elevated NT-proBNP), identify diuretic non-adherence/dietary indiscretion as the precipitant, flag the mildly elevated non-rising troponin as demand-type rather than ACS, and recommend IV loop diuretic plus precipitant workup rather than antimicrobial therapy.
expectedNextQuestions: Adherence to diuretic and heart failure medications, and any recent dose changes?
Dietary sodium/fluid intake in preceding days?
Any chest pain, palpitations, or syncope to suggest ischaemic or arrhythmic precipitant?
Baseline weight and renal function for comparison?
Response of dyspnoea, oxygenation and urine output to initial diuresis?
expectedInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiogram (LVEF, wall motion, valvular function)
Daily weight and fluid balance monitoring

expected.diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, pulmonary congestion

regressionAssertions: contraindications flag NSAID avoidance and cautious diuresis in setting of renal function change
